en: Having bowed down to Nārāyaṇa— the ocean of all perfect qualities, possessing the immeasurable splendor of the high-rising sun, free from every defect, the Lord of All, the Guru praised by Brahmā— I shall expound the meaning of these *Ṛg* verses, which brings great satisfaction, according to this [commentary] of Śrī Madhvācārya. 1.1.
Even that Nārāyaṇa, who is the substratum of all remaining auspicious qualities,
is full, the bestower of prosperity, and possessed of infinite bliss— this is what is proclaimed by his very name.
Therefore, as the progenitor through his qualities, he is to be chosen for the elevation of virtues;
because his nature consists of splendor and knowledge, Bharga is to be meditated upon by all people. (3)
He who impels all intellects is declared to be the meaning of the Gāyatrī;
because of his fullness, he is called Puruṣa and is proclaimed in the Pauruṣa Sūkta. || 4 ||
"He alone is the meaning of the entire Veda, he alone is the meaning of all the scriptures, and he alone is the meaning of all words—thus says the supreme Upaniṣad. (5)
By the specific mention of "these very verses" (tā vā etā ṛcaḥ), the nature of the Ṛgveda is established;
and by the Śruti passage beginning with "yo devānām," the names of the gods are specifically designated.
Because it is manifest as being located therein, one says there that which is named "Agni";
since its nature as fire consists in its leadership (*agraṇītva*), it therefore receives the name "Agra" (the Foremost). || 7 ||
In this very way, the Blessed One Bādarāyaṇa has explained the etymology [of the name], just as words such as "Agni" and others apply to Janārdana. 8.
"Likewise, we shall explain its etymology for the sake of the knowledge-attainment of the wise;
therefore, let this word 'Agni' be honored at the very outset. (9)
He spoke of his preeminence, his leadership, and his role as the guide for those who have fallen; I praise that Lord, who from the very beginning was the benefactor of all. 1.10.
Because he always appoints the priests for sacrifices as their director, and because of his radiance, victory, splendor, praise, and conduct; 11.
Through its movement and through its delight, it is specifically called "divine" (deva) when established in the Hotṛ priest;
for, by virtue of its form as established in fire, Agni is the deity of the Hotṛ.
He who is the Hotṛ among those named Hotṛs, offering the objects of the senses into the fires of the sense-faculties, is called Ratnadhātama because he is the supreme sustainer of delight (rati). 13.
He is to be praised by the past, present, and future ṛṣis known as Vijñāna, as well as by all the gods and others; and he shall bring the gods here.
By that very means, one obtains wealth consisting of property and knowledge, and day by day, there is constant prosperity rather than decline. 15.
And that sacrifice which brings renown along with progeny and is indeed most heroic—
around which you always stand as its protector.
He alone, established on the path of ritual injunction, undoubtedly attains the gods;
he possesses the wisdom that grasps everything in its entirety and is pervaded by all virtuous qualities. 17.
He who restrains even those of foremost renown, the most excellent among the wise;
he who comes to all his devotees, intent upon accepting their worship. (18)
O beloved of the virtuous, whatever auspicious thing you wish to do for the sacrificer,
bring that endeavor to fruition by setting the ritual acts in motion through your own effort alone.
It is indeed true of your limbs that the horse Hari was born from the essence of your body;
for it was from Aṅgiras, the son of Aṅgiras, that Agni once came into being.
Day and night, the name of Vastar is always desired by living beings;
though we are small, by our intellect we [worship] you, the Lord of exalted qualities. 21.
With mental, physical, and verbal acts of devotion,
we offer salutations to You, the Lord of Sacrifice, who shines brilliantly in Your own abode and ever prospers at the ritual.
We approach you, the protector of knowledge according to reality, as we would a father;
be a good refuge for us, just as you are for your own biological son.
Protect [us] always for the sake of continuous happiness or for the sake of perfect reality;
for the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is the Sage of all sciences. 24.
Furthermore, there is the Vedic scripture stating, "He who [created] Brahmā," and another [scripture] declares that the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas are his very breath. (25)
It is clear that from Hayagrīva the radiant words came forth;
such a statement exists in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, and likewise another in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
These vidyās, beginning with Hayagrīva, issued forth as his breath;
they were accepted by Brahmā, and also by Rudra, Śeṣa, and the Vipras. 27.

Dakṣa and the others, Sanaka and the others, Śakra and the others, as well as the Manus, received [these teachings] and, having attained them, they established them throughout the entire universe. || 28 ||
And it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa that the unborn Lord Kapila,
Bādarāyaṇa, dwelling within the heart, proclaimed the sciences to Brahmā.
"The Vidyās, preceded by the syllable Oṃ, impel [all beings] among all things;
they always first belong to Brahman"—thus says the Sāttvata-saṃhitā (1.30).
By the mere utterance once of the recitation, the entire Brahman was grasped through the grace of Vyāsa, who dwells within, and by virtue of his eternal power.
And because he possesses infinite power, it was uttered by him simultaneously;
and because he is the first knower of all, the Sage is Brahmā. (32)
Suparṇa [Garuḍa] is the recipient of all the Vedas, and Nāgarāja [Vāsuki] is the recipient of the Pañcarātra;
because they were the second recipients, they are both proclaimed as sages (muni). || 33 ||
He who perceives the Veda for himself is proclaimed a seer (ṛṣi);
even one who has studied it up to twelve recitations becomes a seer.
The word of the Guru, such as Suparṇa and others, regarding that which has appeared spontaneously [in one's own mind], is for the sake of certainty; it is solely the cause of dharma for Viriñca.
Then Śakra is the seer of the Ṛg-verses, Sūrya alone is that of the Yajus-formulas, and Soma is that of the Sāman-chants; these three are declared to be their respective recipients.
"Agni is the sole seer of the Atharvāṅgirases, and likewise for the Atharvaṇas";
thus have the seers of the collection been stated, as well as those who belong to each individual branch separately. || 37 ||
From the knowledge of this, there shall be the attainment of unseen fruits and happiness; and from the knowledge of the four types of seers, there shall also be worldly success. 38.
And these may be many even for a single person—whether they be hymns or even individual verses—according to the specific attainment of each respective state. (39)
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, or Suparṇa perceives their prayers and so forth in the form of speech, according to the specific distinctions of their respective capacities. (1.40)
Because she possesses pride in all the Vedas, Śrī, Brahmāṇī, and Bhāratī are the seers of all sciences; this has been explained by Brahmā to Marut. 41.
After their own husbands, they are to be seen as distinct from them;
impelled by them, they constantly praise Hari with all their various sciences (vidyās). 42.
Their tradition has been proclaimed through their status as Vedic meters and their status as sages;
and all of them, moreover, are to be remembered individually as sages. (43)
Gāyatrī and Bṛhatī—these are all likewise [the meters of] Garuḍa;
the Brahma-mantras are Anuṣṭubh, Indrāṇī is Triṣṭubh, and Svāhā is also so called. || 44 ||
Gāyatrī, Jagatī, Vāruṇī, and likewise Rohiṇī;
Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Tārā, Paṅkti, and likewise Śacī. || 45 ||
The Uṣṇih is considered the wife of Sūrya, and the Jagatī the wives of all the gods; the Virāj is celebrated as the wife of Mitra and Varuṇa. 46.
All the *aticchandāḥ* meters are proclaimed to be all the goddesses; their name is *virāj*, and they are so designated even when they are deficient or excessive [in syllables]. 47.
The designations *nicṛt*, *bhurik*, and *virāj*, as well as names such as *prastāra* and so forth, are applied;
however, when many [verses] have the same measure, they are given a single name. || 48 ||
And likewise, the presiding deities of all pride and the three types of thirst are, in their respective order, the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, the master of all vidyās. 49.
There, the well-known deities are absent, and here Śrī is likewise absent;
there, Brahmā alone is well-known, and therefore by that sequence [the worlds are named]. (1.50)
Excluding those previously established, the deities are considered to extend up to Śakra;
Brahmā and Vāyu are on the mountain, as are Viṣṇu, Indra, Śeṣa, Rudra, and their wives.
Śakra and Kāma followed Kāmaputra; likewise followed the sons of Dakṣa and Aṅgiras, as well as Śacī, Rati, and the wives of Sūrya, Soma, Dharma, and the others.
Pradhāna, Marut, Vāripati, Agni, and the Maruts;
Nirṛti, the Strīs, Sūrya and the others, as well as the two Aśvins. || 53 ||
Respectively, by one part out of ten, five, a hundred, and an infinite number of crores, and likewise by all the qualities beginning with knowledge, devotion, strength, and sovereignty. (54)
Even in liberation, this sequence indeed persists; these deities have been declared, specifically Indra and the others, each individually by means of their respective signs. 55.
The deities should be placed in their respective positions; this indeed is the supreme rule.
Furthermore, the forms of Keśava are to be fashioned with the syllables of the deities from the Vedas and other scriptures. 56.
By means of both concise and detailed treatment, these [forms] should be described separately according to their intended meaning;
likewise, the other forms should also be explained as appropriate and according to the rule.
In the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā, in the study of the Vedas, and in the Nirukta composed by Vyāsa—all this was indeed spoken by the Lord himself when it had come forth. || 58 ||
All the Vedas and their names, as well as these very Ṛg-verses beginning with "Indra, Mitra, and Varuṇa," have this as their supreme authority. 59.
Having understood the gradations among deities and that Keśava is the most excellent of all, one is indeed liberated from this [bondage]; not otherwise by any means whatsoever.
Thus the Paiṅgi-śruti also says; and here it is seen in every respect that [the text], beginning with "Not you, O greatness," refers exclusively to the Lords (Īśvaras). 61.
The Śruti speaks of the qualities of Viṣṇu and never of his defects in any way;
for even the boundary of Brahman was surpassed by her who was born. 62.
Brahmā did not rejoice at all, nor was he free from fear; he perceived those very same defects in Rudra as those previously mentioned, such as "he did not exist" and so forth.
Whomever I desire, him I make fierce; even for Rudra, I make him a bow.
O you who worship the phallus, do not follow after this god! 64.
"Many such faults have been proclaimed, beginning with 'He slays the gods who worship the phallus' (ghnañchiśnadevān).
Therefore, the womb recoils, thinking, 'I am only this much. (65)
For it has been stated many times that the Goddess has other substrata;
likewise, it is certain from that very source that others also have her as their substratum. 66.
For it is said: "Brahmā alone was in the beginning"; then the birth of Rudra and the others is described, as well as the statement: "Having been born, he encompassed all created things. (67)
Respectfully, she declared that her shadow is both nectar and death;
she is the sovereign over the infinite, and from her came both breath and speech.
From her came Rudra and Umā; from him, Indra; and from him, others.
Thus says the Sauparṇa Śruti, as well as the Saprākṣitiya.
"Vāyu churned for him, for Vāyu who is all the gods"—with these words beginning "He [came] with all the gods," there are also other authorities here. (1.70)
Nārāyaṇa, Aditi, Vāyu, Vāṇī, Rudra, Umā, and Vibhu—each subsequent one among these is inferior by a hundredfold compared to the preceding one, starting from Vāyu. || 71 ||
Thus the *barjūśruti* says; from Śakra comes the *saptākṣitiśruti*.
"This I go to your body"—other [verses] as well are clearly of the same nature. 72.
They say that even Vāyu, Indra, Soma, Hutāśana (Fire), Sūrya, and Rudra—these five gods—are but one Great Soul. (73)
"The Great One (Mahat) creates and devours, and the vital breath (Prāṇa) does so," says the swift Vedic revelation;
"for they have flowed away from the presser [of Soma], they did not regard Indra as a god. (74)
Where the bull-like Vṛṣākapi, my friend among the prosperous, took delight—that Indra of whom [the sage] did not say "He is not Indra," for he was indeed a subordinate of Viṣṇu. (75)

The statement beginning with "He quickened the Vedas" refers to him by the name of Viṣṇu; furthermore, the scriptural passage concerning bliss would indicate that he exists even among living beings. (76)
He said: "Even over the sun, Indra, Vāyu, and Viṣṇu, he exercises lordship;
for the five deities—the sun, the dawn, and [the others]—die. (77)
From his eye came both the sky and the sun;
from his eye the sun was born—thus says the ancient scripture, as do other [scriptures] besides. (78)
From Viṣṇu was born Vāta, from Vāta came Indra, and from him the Sun;
and Soma likewise—thus these three, each preceding one being superior in qualities to the next.
From Viṣṇu, Prāṇa was born; from Prāṇa, Indra, Ravi, and Vidhu; and likewise their dissolution [occurs in reverse order]. Among them, each preceding one is superior in qualities. (1.80)
Turaśruti and Sauparṇī, as well as Piṅgaśruti, are likewise [authoritative];
therefore, Viṣṇu is determined by the collection of Śrutis to be supreme above all. 81.
Therefore, one should declare that speech in which there is a statement of fault to be inferior;
however, the very absence of fault belongs to Viṣṇu, even in those [beings] who are situated in the intermediate state. 82.
There are three meanings in all the Vedas, ten meanings in the entire Mahābhārata,
and even the thousand names of Viṣṇu possess a hundred continuous meanings.
Thus, because the words of Skanda, depending on the distinction of their respective meanings, declare Hari’s faultlessness and the faults of others in turn, [they are authoritative]. (84)

For it is said that virtues heard [in others] are meaningful only when they serve to make known the gradations [of excellence] and the faults [of others]; thus he declared that Hari alone is the absolute locus of all virtues. (85)
Viṣṇu alone is faultless and complete in all qualities, and there is no other;
Māyā alone is devoid of faults, yet she is entirely under his control. (86)
"Brahmā is generally free from defects, while the others are defective in succession"—thus says the venerable Śruti; therefore, a distinction among the objects [of knowledge] is accepted. (87)

Relying solely upon the *rūḍhi* (etymological) sense, one should analyze the meanings in their proper order and bring them into the state of *yoga* (meditative union) with Viṣṇu for the sake of attaining faultless qualities in their fullness. 88.
Thereafter, one should likewise apply [this method] to the others as appropriate;
and thus it was proclaimed by the Lord himself in the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā. (89)
The various forms of Viṣṇu that belong to other deities, as well as those expressed in the hymns (sūkta) dedicated to Agni and others— by these names, there shall be a distinction among the hymns.
The passage beginning with "nakirmākiḥ smasi" is intended to express an excessiveness already stated;
for, when there is excessiveness, the rule "adhikaṃ ca" was indeed proclaimed by Patañjali (Hari). || 91 ||
The forms *kṛtvī* and *hatvī* are used as previously mentioned; furthermore, the third suffix (*ktvā*) is employed in the sense of excellence.
Moreover, *viśliṣṭa* is desired when the meaning is "separated," and *ūna* when the meaning is "diminished. (92)
The reversal [of the order] is declared to occur in the cases of non-differentiation, instrumentality, and sovereignty;
there is non-differentiation among the forms of Hari, as well as among his qualities and actions. (93)
The distinction between its very parts is seen by those liberated ones, beginning with the venerable Brahmā; the distinction from insentient matter follows by logical necessity (kaimutya). || 94 ||
And this has been declared in its entirety in the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā:
that there is no difference whatsoever even among those who are liberated, on account of their own qualities and so forth. (95)
For transmigrating beings as well as for insentient things, there is both difference and non-difference with respect to their qualities;
in the case of the insentient, there is difference in part, and both [difference and non-difference] in their totality.
Human beings, Gandharvas, the hosts of Pitṛs, the Kārmikas, the Tāttvikas, the gods, Śakra, Śiva, and Brahmā are [distinguished] by qualities such as bliss in liberation. 97.
"Always joined with a mutual affection exceeding ten thousand [in degree]," such is the statement contained in the Siddhānta, spoken by the Blessed One himself. 98.
Study of the sacred texts, knowledge of reality, devotion to Viṣṇu, detachment, renunciation of prohibited actions, and the constant performance of prescribed duties. (99)
Constant mindfulness of Viṣṇu alone is the means to liberation;
without these, there can be no liberation, but with these, it will certainly be attained.

Having understood the seers, meters, and deities, as well as the meaning, with devotion, liberation shall come through the study of one's own Veda for one who is dispassionate and mindful of Hari. 101.
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, he who is friendly toward all is called a Brahmin. 102.
Therefore, one should constantly meditate upon Hari and perform one's own sacred study (svādhyāya) with diligence;
for one who is attached [to worldly things], there are enjoyments in this world and the next, but another is liberated.
Thus has the teaching on private recitation been spoken by the Blessed One himself;
however, the fruit of teaching it to others is a thousandfold greater than that of private recitation. 104.
The merit of one who sees the meaning is ten millionfold; that of a director is infinite.
Greater still is the merit of one who establishes the rule through both logic and scripture.
The fruit of the Veda, the seer of all, is said to be complete;
the meaning of the anudātta is indeed stability, while the meaning of the udātta is loftiness. 106.

Lowness is the meaning of the svarita accent; the state of naturalness is that of the pracaya accent; in the samāhāra, all these meanings are combined—this is the established rule for the meanings of the accents. 107.
Due to the difference in the quality of praise, there is a distinction in the accentuation of the word-initial and so forth;
however, this rule is common [to all], wherever such a specific case occurs. (108)
In the same sequence, for others such as the ṛṣis and so forth, according to their respective capacities, there is likewise darkness (tamas) when they speak of a meaning contrary [to reality]. 109.
To whatever extent the instigator possesses knowledge, to that same extent his merit is greater;
likewise, it is the opposite in the case of the contrary [sin]. In both memory and direct knowledge, the result is equal.
Beyond the realms of darkness, hell, humanity, heaven, and liberation, it is said that for all [beings], the fruit [of action] varies according to the gradations of their respective capacities.
Thus has this discourse been delivered even in solitude;
one should clearly understand that an object is known exactly according to the degree of its fitness [to be perceived]. (112)
"Endowed with infinite rules and possessing infinite specific meanings, the Vedas are thus; in brief, this is the rule that has been proclaimed. (113)
Furthermore, another restrictive factor is that [the teaching] occurs within the sentences of the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā*.
Therefore, Brahmā and the others, who impart knowledge, are to be saluted and worshipped. (114)
By virtue of their gravity and through a specific sequence, Keśava is the highest of all, starting from his own guru; indeed, each successive teacher is Viṣṇu himself.
The absence of sprouts [of duality] in other [levels] is proclaimed in the *Gurutattva* in due order.
This being the case, [one should worship] Viṣṇu residing in Agni, and also the one named Agni himself. (116)
With a hundred Ṛks of Madhucchandas, he praises Vāyu and the others, together with Agni and the rest, each by their respective names, with true devotion. || 117 ||
Because of its power and because it does not decay, it is called "Vāyu";
or it is known as "Vātyāyu" due to its knowledge, its enveloping nature, and its state of being a support. 118.

Because of the departure (*vyaya*) from this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and so forth, or because one departs (*vāti*) within it, it is called *vāyu*; furthermore, *vaya* also signifies excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*). (119)
Those qualities exist in their entirety and primarily in Vāsudeva;
in others, they are considered to exist according to their respective fitness, provided they are not explicitly excluded.
Because he possesses that vision which is worthy of being seen, this all-pervading Lord is omniscient;
others, however, have minds adorned by devotion and the like, yet they are surpassed by him as gold surpasses silver.
Since these pressed juices, adorned with gold, are offered to Vāyu, protect them and hear my invocation; even this [grammatical] transposition occurs for the sake of independence. 122.
The mind, too, is an object of enjoyment for the Lord solely by virtue of His mere pleasure;
for that alone is the true meaning of the Veda, by which there may be a preponderance of excellence. 123.
Because it is the instigator, and because others lack the fruit, [the scripture] has that [instigator] as its purpose;
for wherever the beginning and other [criteria] point, that alone is the intended meaning. 124.
Just as those who know the sacrifice praise with hymns and recitations according to the rule, so too speech, when joined with you, brings about the desired object for the sake of the sacrifice. 125.
Because of its great purpose, this Soma-drinking rite is exceedingly vast; and Indra, on account of his supreme sovereignty, has directed it toward you alone. 126.
It may be that this [name] arose because it was seen as radiant, or because "it bestows" (rāti);
for the gods who have Soma as their presiding deity and who go toward Soma desire these two. || 127 ||
Because he was approached by his beloved ones, he is Upendra; because he is Saṅkarṣaṇa, he is Hari. Due to his dual form, there is a plurality, which arises solely from his specific manifestations.
In this matter, one should not suspect any difference whatsoever in Hari alone;
He is indeed one without a second, and here there exists nothing diverse. 129.
He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity.
Just as water rained upon a mountain slope flows away in different directions, so he who perceives the various dharmas as separate runs after them alone. 1.130

Having thus stated the dharmas of distinctness through their very negation, a distinction is known from the Śruti; and moreover, from the witness [of the sun], it is known that the two remain forever in the sun, the lord of food, for one who understands. 131.
For one who knows, the two sons are ever situated in the sun, the lord of food.
The repetition [of the mantra] is desired as an indicator of intense devotion, flowing swiftly and intensely.
Sacrificing, praising, and performing actions that follow what has been done is itself the atonement. With such a disposition, they should quickly approach Him, O immovable ones.
Since those two are indestructible, the term [“man”] may be used figuratively in certain instances,
just as the immortality of the gods is well-established;
for this Mitra is so called because he measures and protects, or because he makes the days measured.
Or because he bestows what is measured (*mitam rāti*), or because he eternally delights what is measured (*mitam ramayati*);
|| 135 || Or because he veils (*āvṛṇoti*) through darkness, even out of ignorance; thus he is *Varuṇa*.
Or because he raises up what is excellent (*varam unnayati*), or because he is the bliss of excellence (*varānanda*); || 136 ||

He is called Pūtadakṣa because his skill (dakṣa) is purified (pūta) by this [knowledge]. I invoke him who is blissful, for from whom peace and joy proceed. He is celebrated as Riśādā because he is the enjoyer of perfect happiness. 137
Hari is called *ghṛta* because of his supreme purity, and *ghṛtācī* because she pleases him;
Viṣṇu is the perfect accomplisher of the self-study (*svadhyāya*) of his devotees according to their true nature.
That Blessed Lord is eternally increasing, not figuratively, but by virtue of the Truth itself.
If [it is argued that] the two others are not denotable by the word *veda* because they touch upon the *ṛta*, then the Blessed One is the *ṛta*.
[The root] *ṛ* means "to go"; because he is present within all things, he is the *ṛta*.

In the *Saṃhitā*, however, lengthening and so forth are prescribed when there is an increase [of syllables] within a word; otherwise, it is for the purpose of making known that there is no other meaning, as in "īśāthe" and "mahākratum.
Or rather, [it serves to indicate] "great happiness" (*mahat sukham*) or "one who conquers many" (*tuvijau*), being born of Brahman (*brahmajātau*), and of such a nature.
Likewise, Hari is called "sthāna" (the place) because he is the reality itself, while "kṣaya" (destruction) refers to this world.
Both of them—Karma and the agent, or Dakṣa and the agent alone—constantly bestow these upon us; they are eternally subject to increase and decrease, coming and going.
O Aśvins, lords of auspiciousness, with swift hands, possessing many cattle and eating much, provide us with foods fit for sacrifice;
or else, quickly bestow upon us our own shares from the sacrificial offerings. 144
They are called Aśvins because they move swiftly, or because they possess horses due to their rapid understanding;
likewise, they are Aśvins because they pervade everything through their horse-like nature.
They perform many deeds with an intellect whose essence is happiness and vigor, and [they possess] speech.
O you two who possess wisdom, enjoy these our offerings, you who are the refuge of all;
for you, O Dasras, are the destroyers of all enemies and indeed our kinsmen.
These pressed Soma juices are for you both—the swift ones for whom the sacrificial grass has been praised.
The two *nāsatyas* reside in the nose (*nāsikā*) and are never possessed of bad qualities (*asat-guṇa*).
Rudra is so called because of his destruction (*rujāṃ dravaṇataḥ*) [of diseases], while Vāyu is so named because he follows after that [Rudra].
Alternatively, he is so called because of his moisture (*sneha*), because of his submissiveness (*anuvaśatva*), or because he moves along their path (*tanmārgagati*). || 148 ||
By the Śruti passage "In whom shall I [abide]?", Vāsudeva and the two Aśvins are also indicated;
they are expressed by the words *rudravartani* and *citraṃ bhadraṃ rataṃ citau*.
This is because they are to be removed from *cidrata* (the delight in consciousness), or because there is no difference between them and *cita* (consciousness) due to their devouring nature.
The Blessed One is supreme because his knowledge consists of such rays;
he is called Citrabhānu because the Lord’s splendor is like that.
These Somas are your desires, woven with cloths of fine threads.
And their minds have been purified by expanded, subtle means of knowledge.
The deities residing in the rays of the moon and within the minds are the servants of the Moon;
Hari alone is the sovereign lord of the entire Moon.
Whether requested by our own intellect, or impelled by his own intellect,
or urged by the Brahmins with devotion, let the Hotṛ priest speak directly the Vedic hymns associated with Soma for the sake of the sacrificer who desires them. (153)
Moreover, any practitioner whatsoever who is considered a performer of sacrifice—whether that sacrifice be mental or verbal—and he who is the invoking priest (hotṛ) calling upon the deities;
as well as he who is impetuous and striving, withdrawing the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). 154.
It functions by means of which, like Indra (Hari) with his bay horses (haribhiḥ);
or else, because of the seizing (haraṇa) of the sense-objects, the vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) are called "bay horses" (harayaḥ).
Since it functions within them, or since it causes one to go toward them, [it is so called]. 155–156.
The word *harivā* or *harivān* means "possessing Viṣṇu," or it exists as such; *canaḥ* and *manaḥ* are said here to mean "pleasure," and *sukham* is expressed in some instances.
Furthermore, those [words] beginning with *ā* and *omā* are proclaimed as being used in the sense of "accepted" (*svīkṛta*) on all sides.

The Blessed Viṣṇu is called *Oṃ*; by him the gods were created. He is woven (*ota*) within measures (*māna*), and he is indeed woven (*prota*) within those things to be measured (*meya*); thus he is declared to be *Omā*.
Subjects (*prajā*) are called *ṛṣaṇayaḥ*, and they are the *viśve* because of their entry (*praveśana*).

Or how could the sound "vā" belong to all the people (viś) or to the non-people (avi)? To whom would it apply? [The word] *dātāraḥ* refers to the givers or the sacrificers; *apturaḥ* refers to those impelled by their actions.
*Usrāḥ* are the rays of light, and *svasarāṇi* are the days. 1.160–161.
O gods, since you have no attachment to saṃsāra due to your certainty of liberation,

possessing the certain knowledge of what is desired, and being free from all illusion in this world— since you are without suffering and without malice, may you graciously accept our sacrifice, O Cloud-like ones. 161.
The fires (vahnayaḥ) are so called because they carry [the oblation]; they are purifiers (pāvakāḥ) because of their cleansing nature.
Or, because of his movement (saraṇāt) through all-pervasiveness, Hari is the All-Knowing One (sarvajñaḥ), the "Sara.
Or, because she possesses that quality of flowing (saratitvāt), Sarasvatī is indeed "possessing flow" (sarasā).
The qualities are the "lake" (saras), while the Goddess is that which expresses Hari.
Alternatively, because he is dear to Hari, Vāyu is "possessing a lake" (sarasvān), or his beloved is so;
or else, because he is pervasive by virtue of his qualities, the Blessed Lord is Sarasvatī. 163–164.
The Blessed One possesses both female form and male form, yet he is not neuter;
because he is free from the defects of both female and male, he is nonetheless the object of those terms.
Furthermore, the Lord of horses is called "Vājinī" (the possessor of mares), while the Sun is called "Vājini" (the possessor of horses).
Or rather, she is called Vājinī because she is the mistress of the Vājin meters;
since the meters are her horses, she possesses them as other mares possess their stallions.
Alternatively, she is Vājinī because speech (Vāk) is possessed of food (anna), or because it consists of the battle of knowledge. || 166-167 ||
May her son Vāguma, her daughter Vājinīvatī, Sarasvatī, or even Hari swiftly carry our sacrifice;
for the Goddess is always a giver of food, since she dwells together with wisdom (dhī). 168.
She who is enriched by wisdom, eternally awakened, and the constant inspirer of eloquent speech—she alone, through her sovereignty, may have her [dualistic] states dissolved;
in this very manner, she alone is the sustainer of sacrifices and other rites. (1.169–170)
The great ocean is the Supreme Brahman, because it is splendor (tejas) and because of its greatness (mahattva);
the syllable 'A' signifies bliss, and the syllable 'Ṇa' indeed denotes liberation.
That Goddess, having bestowed the most exalted knowledge, makes that known. 171

The great ocean, the God himself, illuminates his own self and causes all intellectual insights to shine forth by bestowing excellent knowledge. (172) A hymn (*sūkta*) is said to be recited without interruption, whereas a prose passage (*anuvāka*) belongs to a single moment of time.
And there would be a change in those [mantras] due to the insertion or deletion of verses;
therefore, Bādarāyaṇa composed those two [the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda] in order to demonstrate the infinity of the Vedas.
Having extracted the verses from the verses, that Lord fashioned the Ṛgveda.
The Yajus-mantras were extracted from the Nigadas, and likewise the Sāmans from the Sāman;
thus, according to the words of the Purāṇas, these Ṛks were drawn out here and there and attained the status of Śākhās by the disciples and their pupils.
In the verses beginning with "mānas tena," a deficiency is observed in meaning within the preceding [recensions];
furthermore, some verses spoken by Śunaḥśepa are recited elsewhere.
Here too, since the observation is made out of sequence, there would not be a single uniform order.
However, because the Vedas are infinite, the Lord, for the most part in accordance with ritual action,
made a compendium; and by his authorization, his disciples likewise made divisions into eight sections, chapters, and verses, which he himself also established.
Therefore, for the sake of providing rest during private recitation (svādhyāya), there is an inversion of the sequence;
in various places, even the supplementary texts (khilas) are seen as interspersed.
Furthermore, where no difference in meaning exists, there is the insertion of other words.
Wherever there is even the slightest distinction, not a single word shall be omitted.
For the sake of accomplishing one’s desired aims, one should worship Viṣṇu, the creator of beautiful forms;
or for protection, like a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu), for the milking of that which resides within him. || 1.180–181 ||
Day after day we invoke you by your own name, for you are the supreme bestower of knowledge upon one who is endowed with the vehicle called wisdom,
or even one possessed of gold and other riches.
Since you are the source of happiness, may we therefore obtain your excellent favor.
Indeed, our thoughts directed toward you are already most excellent;
do not look upon us with eyes moistened by compassion as if we were something beyond that. Whether it be my mind or Śakra, even though the Supreme Lord is far away—
Let those who have gone to Him— who is ungraspable, imperishable, and all-pervading—
and who are His constant, supreme friends, as well as those who have reached Him from elsewhere, speak of that God to us. (184) Let them also speak to us of Him.
Even those who, departing from us out of ignorance, offer service to the Lord alone,
they too shall call upon our Supreme Lord as their very life-breath.
Even our enemies shall always speak of us as fortunate subjects.
May we remain under the favor and happiness of you, Indra, the piercer of enemies.
Quickly bring into your own belly, or with satisfaction into your heart, this swift Soma— possessing your very speed and even swifter than thought— which is the ornament of the sacrifice.
"This very [drink] is the cause of the pride that leads to such acts as flying up, and it is the cause of the dullness [of the mind] when one proceeds before the eyes of one's friends;
having drunk this, you have become possessed of great knowledge, yet remain unenveloped by darkness. (188)
Through grace alone, [the Lord] is dense with the darkness that is difficult to overcome for those who are liberated;

for indeed, by the very removal of obscuration, He protects from the "Vrtras"—that is, the ignorances—the man who offers food, as well as the warrior in battles, the devotee, and the man of knowledge. 1.190–191.
We shall fight you so that we may obtain the wealth of knowledge and the like;
sing for that Indra, who is the earth of all riches, the giver of happiness, and the shore beyond this cycle of existence, from whom our enemies—ignorance and the rest—have fled. 191.

The trembling [of the earth] was proclaimed by the conjunction of the Moon and the Sun as occurring either when all the planets tremble somewhere, or out of ancient shame, or due to a distinct state of invincibility;
it is the most perfect among the perfectly full, the sovereign of those worthy of choice. 192. Supūrṇānāṃ pūrṇatamaṃ vareṇyānāmadhīśvaram.
When the Soma has been pressed, sing with ease to that Lord;
let there be no exertion for yoga in any respect—this "na" is used in the sense of restriction.
He alone is the Blessed One, the knower of wisdom, and He is present within the intellect.
Buddhi is called Purandhi because she was formerly the refuge [of the gods], or else because she is the wife [of Indra].
If, however, the term refers to a wife, then her purpose [as such] would not accompany him along with the food offerings (195)— he,
at whose very presence even his enemies do not dare to look upon the tip of his hair.

Because it seizes the objects of the senses before them, the mind (manas) is called "Hari"; and because it likewise [seizes] them, the intellect (buddhi) is also denoted by the word "Hari. Darkness and the other qualities are its enemies. For one who drinks the Soma, the pure Somas mixed with curds are for the sake of attainment.
Their minds always turn toward Hari, being absorbed in meditation.

O Lord, you who are eternally full with auspicious knowledge, you who are never manifested by hunger or other such needs, you have been surrounded by our songs for the sake of manifesting your preeminence and for the attainment of a son.
"O Lord, may the sons who are born to this [king], being your servants with exalted minds,
manifest our songs even more fully— just as the *stomas* manifest in the *sāmans*, and the *ukthas* in the *ṛks*— through their great virtues. (198–199)
The expansion [of Viṣṇu] must be like the expansion of space-consciousness, and not otherwise;
for the Śruti has proclaimed of him: "He does not increase, nor does he become smaller.
(1.200) Furthermore, because it would contradict the primary purport [of the scriptures], there can be no other meaning than that of the Śruti.

If his increase and lordship were dependent upon something else, how could he possess "undecaying abundance"? For it is from this state that his full intention is said to arise. May he also receive from us that strength which bestows infinite fruit.
Or rather, let Him grant human powers, wherein all capacities reside.
Therefore, because His power is infinite, increase and the like do not apply to Him in any way.
With this meaning in mind—that He is endowed with everything—the King of the Vedas has said: [He is] "endowed with all. (202–203)
May no mortals ever be the slayers of our bodies;
O Lord, remove that slaughter by granting us liberation from it. (204) Thus, among humans, may there be no calamities for our bodies.
In due time, death shall come to him from a divine cause, for he is devoid of a physical body.
As for the manly deeds of Vāsudeva: they always yoke the ancient sun, the radiant maker of day, as Aruṇa moves around the mountains.

By those very powers, they cause other things such as the moon and the sun to shine in heaven; and his own powers—his mind and intellect—yoke the two bay horses (harī) for him, either as objects of desire or by virtue of their superior qualities. 207.
O gods, just as two horses yoked to a chariot are always exceedingly swift, so too do they apply their own mind and intellect to this body;
they employ them within the body and establish the sun and other luminaries therein.
Furthermore, Brahmā and the others shall always be the establishers of the sun and other celestial bodies.
The two horses are said to be ruddy and tranquil, for they always bring about the attainment of happiness.
They are dark-brown at the head and ruddy [at the neck]; these two are known as the foremost steeds of Śakra.

Both of them, carrying that Lord toward the one who perceives [the truth], act with true knowledge regarding Him, even as He remains unknown. And the Lord, through His powers which abide and shine forth, has attained manifestation for both gold and non-gold.

Even though subject to death, the gods, by the will of Hari, immediately thereafter obtained happiness and once again attained their state of divinity. By the mere will of the Supreme Lord, even the deities possess powers.
Bestowing upon the sacrifice that which is to be proclaimed, and indeed even the firm name of Viṣṇu, he— who,
though remaining hidden in the cave, shatters all things with his own powers and sustains the entire world— has attained states of luminosity.
He obtained [this] with favor along with such gods as these;
they, perfectly illuminating this form of his intellect as it truly exists, praised him—who was wealthy, great, and renowned—with beautiful words. || 214-215 ||
Śaṅkara himself came together with him for the very purpose of seeing him,
as did Puruhūta, whose essence is sacrifice, and Śrī and Bhūmi, who are the embodiments of bliss,
along with the beloved hosts of gods endowed with faultless, great wisdom. (216)

And together with Vāyu, they worship the Supreme Lord because of their great wisdom. For this reason, O all-pervading one, come here from heaven or from the solar orb, presiding over our sacrifice for us who go everywhere.
In this [context], the words attain their meaning perfectly and in the most primary sense.
In the passage "yuñjanti," because of its frequent occurrence, the term "devayantaḥ" is also [implied];
for, based on what is observed due to such frequency, no other meaning is intended apart from the words themselves. (218–219)
We recognize him as the one who bestows gain in the form of prosperity, whether from this heaven or the netherworld,
or from the great and enchanting world of Viṣṇu.
Him alone the singers of the Gāthās praise with the Sāman chants, and the Bahvṛcas with the Ṛg verses.

Even by means of great words of praise, he is united with the two bay horses (haryoḥ) in the chariot; or rather, for the two yogins, he is joined through the mere faculty of speech within the mind and intellect.
He is indeed the wielder of the thunderbolt (vajrī), possessing both ease and bliss, for his nature consists of the element of knowledge-bliss (jñānānanda).
Beneficial, delightful, and described as golden,
he caused the sun to ascend in the sky for a long time to be beheld;
and one should unify the self of the vital breath with the knowledge that is worthy of reverence.
May He who always protects us in battles fought against many,
even when we are beset by wicked and fierce enemies with evil intentions seeking great wealth— may we invoke Him, the adversary of all foes and the opponent of darkness. 224.
O Bull among men, O giver of all, you who are without rival, unveil that blissful food, our sacrificial offering (caru), which leads to liberation;
for it is through your very impulsion that superior [understandings] arise here and there.

Even those hymns would not attain the state of being well-praised nor reach infinity. Just as a formidable bull, a leader of the herd, moves fearlessly toward the cattle, so does the Lord draw forth the hosts and impel His subjects.
Indeed, even a small thing is fit to serve as an illustration simply by virtue of its being well-known:
"He alone who is the sole lord of riches and of subjects [is called a king].
This is further distinguished according to the divisions of gods, gandharvas, daityas, ancestors, and humans.
We shall also correctly proclaim the five classes of beings, both in their general and specific characteristics,
as well as that which is all-pervading in its manifest form.
For the sake of your welfare, may that Absolute remain alone within you.

Always maintain that most excellent and great wealth, which is ever-powerful, accompanied by victory, and joined with gain; it is for the purpose of protection. By means of this, one conquers enemies through hand-to-hand combat and darkness through the battle of knowledge.
Impelled by you, we shall restrain some [impurities] through horses and other means;
thus, by the very repetition of the prefix, there will be a repetition of the action.
Impelled by you, we shall take hold of the delight in knowledge with firmness.
"May we, with you as our leader, overcome the enemies who attack us with their skilled warriors.

Since Mahat is beginningless and Viṣṇu is the individual soul (jīva) and the lower [nature], let that [Mahat] alone possess greatness; one should not conceive of it as being the Brahman of the individual soul.
In its vastness, that corpse is like space, as is its power of bliss. Those people who have reached Janārdana even by means of being carried by another are truly men; all others are merely beasts.
Even Brahmins who are devoid of wisdom are considered as foolish as Śūdras.
That which is the belly of that God, like the ocean,
pours forth all desires for the devotee, just as great waters satisfy all.
The palate of that [Vṛtra] is his tongue, which exists in many forms within his many mouths.
In this very way, his speech—the great Veda—is likewise known;
like a ripe branch, it yields fruit for the sacrifice and bestows boons upon the exuberant one.
For those who sacrifice to you immediately, even though you are most powerful,
there are always protections and manifestations for one such as me who possesses knowledge;
likewise, the hymns and recitations are always desirable for him.
The Geyas and Śaṃsyas are for the drinking of Soma; one should not drink otherwise.
Since you are a drinker of Soma and possess the joints of Soma, everything will be according to your wish. Through your power, you shall always obtain exhilaration and happiness as your desired goal.
He created him [as Viṣṇu] in the moon; that Viṣṇu is the one who causes intoxication.
He is perfectly fit for Mandin and for Viṣṇu, the performer of all rites for the sake of the performer of all rites.
Together with the protection of ourselves—our own bliss, the lord of the life of the universe, and the non-intoxicated one—he [is established].
The words of the Vedas, issued forth by you, are directed toward you alone without ceasing;
properly released with loud and clear articulation toward their own Lord,
they are unwearied in the form of praise, to be served by you and not by anyone else.
Turn toward us and bestow upon us excellent wealth;
for you alone possess in particular that preeminent, auspicious, and imperishable [fortune].
[Bestow it] upon us, who are zealous, renowned, and worthy of praise.
In this matter, O great king, O you of great fame, urge us on! Bestow upon us ever-increasing and inexhaustible wisdom;
grant us vast knowledge, renown, embodied prosperity, and abundant gain.
Do not urge that there is tautology in this prayer; therefore, once again,
we invoke here the Lord of the Vasus and of the Vasus, the Sovereign of the Gods, the Master,
chanting the Vedic hymns for the attainment of our desired goal.
The indestructible one has been proclaimed for the sake of great strength and happiness;
for every libation poured, he offers praise to the great God who dwells in the true abode.
The chanters of Sāman sing with their hymns, and the knowers of the Ṛgveda recite the verses beyond measure.

The creators (Virincau), O possessor of vast knowledge, recognized you—who are as exalted as the raised banner of Indra—as even more exalted than they in the exercise of power; for by that [power], you perceive the object even beyond that [exalted state]. Thus, you are "Bhavan" (the Existent).
Possessing hidden power, he shines through the multitude of both liberated and unliberated beings.
Since that very agency, extending from Brahmā upwards to the highest levels,
has become abundant and manifest, he is therefore the Supreme Lord.
He perceives all objects and acts with a great troop. Harness the two bay horses, Keśin, who fill the chariot-boxes with their vigor;
then, having approached, hear our words and respond to our hymn of praise.
Offer praise and raise a sound once more with even greater joy;
remaining both within and without, increase our Vedic sacrifice.
Since Viṣṇu is eternally increasing, his manifestation is indeed his own growth.
Crushing his many enemies, Hari, the slayer of the Danujas,
has established himself among us and raised his voice for our friendship,
just as the officiating priest, established among the Soma-pressing priests, raises his voice for the sake of the sons.
We eternally seek refuge in Him alone for the sake of friendship and other benefits;
because His nature is power and bliss, He is Śakra (the Powerful) who is capable in all things, and He proceeds ever bestowing wealth upon us. 255
Indeed, clarity, excellence, and timeliness are the very glory bestowed by you;
reveal the hidden mass of knowledge and grant us prosperity.
(256) Because he is worthy of respect, he is a mountain (adri); because he sustains that [knowledge], he is the vital breath (prāṇa), thus "the mountain-sustainer" (adrivān).
Hari and Śakra, as well as the mountains, [are unable to restrain you] because of your cutting and obstructing;
for neither the two worlds (Heaven and Earth), nor Prosperity and the Earth together, can reach you while you are thus enraged and growing in power, unless you show them favor.
May you conquer the waters and subjects who possess happiness through the vision of You;
shake forth all forms of knowledge and attain even the highest ones Yourself.
O You whose ears have heard much, listen with reverence to this invocation.
This very day, bestow upon me your words and accept the hymn composed by me.
Out of favor, grant me what is dear; we know you to be the most powerful of all.
We call upon you, the listener, for protection, as we invoke you in battles.
Regarding the statement "the highest gain is [attained] by staying in another place," Madhucchandas praised Indra—who was seen going to a sacrifice—by means of two verses beginning with "atūna";
thus, the *Śatarcins* are not in contradiction with that very [praise]. (262)
Because he was grasped by his mother with *kuśa* grass at birth, he became known as Kauśika;
likewise, because he sang (*gāthitvāt*) or because he resided within the golden egg (*hiraṇyāṇḍakośasthatvāt*), he is Hari. May he be ever-joyful and grant us long life.
Make me a sage who gains a thousandfold, and let these songs of mine always surround you; may my words, which take the form of prosperity, be pleasing to you as all-yielding,
and may they be for us in the form of service.
Furthermore, while performing austerities elsewhere, he beheld eight Ṛcas;
thus, through his great excellence, there was a manifestation of such qualities that those first gifts were held in high esteem. (266)
They do not distinguish nor do they perceive food consisting of cattle, nor fame;
if the Lord grants strength, the intellect becomes directed toward lower states.
For the root of darkness is indeed the hole of speech that perceives the meaning of words as something other than what it is.
You opened that door by revealing it and warding it off;
for the gods, freed from fear and impelled by you alone, protected with their true speech the [truth] being obscured by the words of the Daityas. ||268-269||

In ancient times, for the sake of Indra’s Gosava sacrifice, cows protected by Saramā were released even upon the earth; however, they were seized by the Daityas. Having declared her sisterhood to her, [Indra] caused her to drink the remnants of the cow's milk.
For that purpose, those Daityas known as the Paṇis, who were full of strength,
were subsequently slain by Indra after he learned of Saramā's deed;
having kicked her with his foot, she fled from his mouth out of fear as the water flowed away.
Having sent away those who had sought refuge as envoys of the Paṇis,
he then broke through that Girivraja where the cows were stationed;
those cows were brought out, and he indeed performed the Gosava sacrifice.
Then the gods, having approached, protected their lord on all sides.
"By your gifts, I have come again to the river Sindhu;
addressing you with words of praise, I am prepared for the initiation of the sacrifice. (273-274)
The performers who know you, praised by their hymns, wait upon you;
with your powers, you, the powerful one, overcame Vṛtra, the witherer. Or rather, those devoted to wisdom know you as darkness, and they [attain] fame.
Bestow upon us higher knowledge; they praise you with vigor.
From the private recitation of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, from the compendium composed by Vyāsa, and likewise from the honor accorded to the Brāhmaṇas, those who are the sages here have been proclaimed.
Because there is no direct scriptural statement (śruti) and because there is no indicative mark (liṅga), no other sage is understood [as the author].
As long as the absence of śruti and liṅga persists, the prior authority remains. However, by means of the subsequent hundred verses, [one knows] the infallible one named Vahni.
Medhātithi saw eight more [daughters] beyond them who were similar to those;
once, while wandering elsewhere engaged in asceticism, he beheld them.
If the difference in time and place is taken into account, their number would be greater than that calculated. (1.279–280)
Even if those who have gone to other places and been seen elsewhere were to be included here,

they would still fall outside this enumeration, because they were sent by the gods to this place for the sake of a share in the sacrifice. (281) Because [they were] sent by the gods to this place for the sake of a share in the sacrifice.
Agni is the messenger and Vāsudeva; he accomplishes whatever is requested.
He is the knower of all, the omniscient, the knower of sacrifice, and the one whose ritual is the sacrifice itself.
The venerable son of Jamadagni is celebrated by the name Agni.
Due to its multiplicity of forms, repetition (vīpsā) is indeed appropriate for it.
By means of *havīmabhiḥ*—that is, by the invocations of the Ṛg-verses—they invoked Prajāpati.
Being born and being manifested, that which is cut off (*vṛktam*) is said to be spread out (*prastṛtam*).
The sacrificer, having spread the sacrificial grass, desires to awaken the hundred gods.
You sit together with the gods for him whose oblation is well-prepared ghee;
burn up the injurious, devouring Rākṣasa folk.
Into whose mouth oblations are offered, that fire is kindled by the Supreme Lord;
or else, the Āhavanīya fire is kindled by means of friction.
He is the one whose nature is truth, who possesses excellent qualities, the destroyer of suffering, and the dispeller of disease.
It may be a dispeller [of evil] or a bringer of time; "devavīti" is its designation. O you who cause others to dwell, always show mercy to him who dwells with you;
for the sake of your worship, summon the gods who take pride in their senses.
Being praised with the Gāyatrī meter, bestow upon us visible wealth,
as well as food accompanied by sons and endowed with heroism;
choose our hymn of praise with your blazing splendor and the invocations of the Viśvedevas.
"O Tanūnapāt, having summoned the gods for our oblation, perform the sacrifice with reverence.
From that [oblation], the god Vāk became manifest; therefore he is called Tanūnapāt.
Narāśaṃsa is to be praised by men, or else he is another body of Agni. 1.290–291.

Because he is beneficial to the Manus, he is called Manu-hita; therefore, spread the sacrificial grass (barhis) everywhere as a place for the God in due order. For that which is the station of the pure Viṣṇu is indeed the mind, whose back is anointed with clarified butter (ghṛtapṛṣṭha).

Where there may be the vision of Viṣṇu, whose nature is eternally immortal; where the divine Doors, who increase through the sacrifice and are enriched by Hari in the form of the seasons—those Doors, the female servants of Śrī, may they take refuge here in our sacrifice. ||293-294||
Whether in a mental sacrifice or an external one, because he is unattached and non-existent [in the ordinary sense],
he is indeed truly sacrificing this very day;
for that Blessed One is the very gateway for one who desires liberation.
He may be in female form at night, yet he is not truly night, since he is present everywhere;
because Uṣas is of the nature of light, O Subhadrā, I invoke you both.
May the two divine Hotṛ-priests also take their place upon this sacred grass for the sake of the ritual's completion.
Being churned, he is indeed another fire, or the cow, or Hari;
existing in two forms as both the Self and the Inner Self, he always presides over this sacrifice of ours among the gods who perform the rite. ||297-298||
Because he is worthy of praise, Hari is Śrī; she herself is the other form known as Bhū. Mahī is named Bhāratī, while the other belongs to Vāyu and Brahmā.
Hari likewise exists either as merged with them in such forms or as standing apart from them. (299)
Tvaṣṭṛ is so called because of his brilliance (*tejas*), and Viṣṇu because of his power (*bala*). He is called Viśvarūpa because he creates all forms, and Pūrti because of his fulfillment.
He is called Vanaspati because he has fallen into that which is desirable (*vananīya*).
Knowledge is consciousness; "svāhā" is remembered as that which possesses its own portion and course.
Because it is imperishable, it is "amoṣa," and because it milks all desires, it is remembered as "duvas.
Or, Bṛhaspati is the Lord of the Great (Bṛhatī) Speech. ||301-302||
He is Mitra because he is a friend; he is Varuṇa [as well]. He is named Pūṣan because of his nourishing (poṣaṇa).

Or, he is called Bhaga because of his fullness, due to his possession of complete sovereignty and other such qualities. Because he stands at the beginning (ādi), he is Āditya; or he is so called because he goes taking away (ādadāna).
And because of their manifold forms, and because they are spoken of as measures (māna), they are the Maruts.

They are called *matsaras* because they cause exhilaration (*mada*). The subsequent word [is used] in the sense of habitual action. They are *drapsas* because of their flowing; and being situated in the *camasa* vessels, they are *camūṣadas*.
The head is said to be the sacrificial cup (camasa), and likewise the moons [are so called] because they bestow desired objects.
The sacrificer (yajamāna) is "one who desires protection" (avasyu), due to his engagement in the act of protecting.
Or, it may be in the plural referring to those residing within the self, or here it refers to the many sages.
The Lord himself speaks as the speaker of the Uttara [Upanishads]:
"He is the perfecter, the over-performer, and indeed the embellisher.
Or, like horses with glossy backs, they are mounted by the faultless Hari.
"Those who, through mere thought, yoke [the horses] and bring you and the gods—
sacrifice to those gods with praises, strengthened by the known Brahman;
yoke them with their consorts to come, and let them drink the honeyed mead."
