He established incomparable fame both within our hearts and among other superhuman beings on all sides;
he spread his own glory even among ignorant mortals. 111.
Desiring the Great Wisdom and the Supreme Lord, my daughters go forth in every direction, just as cows follow the sound of their own horns;
you cook for me, like a fire, the full honey of bliss situated in liberation.
"Let us speak further on that, since you are always dear to me.
I beheld him, the omniscient one, and his chariot standing upon the earth; he accepted my words, and desiring to protect you, I spoke them. (113-114)
Behold this; you and I—you, the wise king of the universe—being intelligent and mindful of both heaven and earth, listen to us at this time.
Therefore, quickly release us from the threefold bonds and sever them at once.
Then, becoming intent upon the worship of all the gods, he praised Viṣṇu abiding in Agni and Agni himself with words concerning Agni:
"Put on excellent garments and adorn yourself with ornaments. (116)
Performing a great festival, offer our sacrifice. O eternal, pure Lord Hari, O ever-ruling Master of various enjoyments,
or rather, perform the sacrifice for us within yourself, for those people who are full of vigor.

Because he causes delight on the auspicious path, he is called *adhvara* and *makha*. May our speech, along with our prayers and thoughts, lead us eternally to the highest state through its pervasion in heaven and by virtue of reaching all the gods.
The youngest among the ten gods, Viṣṇu, is the bearer of oblations; he resides within that [body]. For my sake, as a friend and a son, he sacrifices to the deities.
He is my kinsman, my attainable lord, and because of his service to me, he is my protector.
For my sake, indulge in intoxication, or intoxicate yourself through your own independence;
for when we sacrifice to all the gods extensively and perpetually, the oblation is indeed offered unto you alone—therefore, become beloved. 121
May Agni, the son of Vāyu, who is pleasant, intoxicating to women and men alike,
and bestows delight and happiness upon us— he who is manifested by the venerable Vāyu, who possesses a multitude of flames, and whose mouth is like that of a mare— grant us well-being. 122.
Since Viṣṇu, who is the submarine fire (Vaḍavāmukha),
is his own exemplar, may that son of Vāyu (Śavasa), the one of vast knowledge who bestows great favor,
be a bringer of happiness to us; or rather, may our Lord himself be our son.

Because you are manifested together with the wind, you are most gracious and of a very blissful nature. From nearby, protect us from the one who seeks to harm us; as the eternal one, present in every dwelling, and possessing all life, accept this hymn of praise.
Speak with reverence to the gods of her who is the essence of charity, whose nature is giving, whose self is the Gāyatrī meter, who is ever-new, and most excellent in hymns;
may she bring us to enjoyments that range from the highest to the lowest and the middle. 126.
Knowledge is said to be the final [aim] because it is the protector of the training for the sake of the true nature of reality,
and because it is the measure for liberation at the end.
Situated near the waves of the milk-ocean, it bestows the portion of liberated enjoyment.
For the sacrificer, you immediately flow forth all that is desired;
because of your eternally supreme splendor, Hari is remembered as Citrabhānu (the one of variegated light).
O All-pervading Lord, whichever mortal you protect and whom you impel in battles, [he succeeds].
Whether consisting of knowledge or ignorance, he is the eternal possessor of true bliss;
or rather, he is the eternal enjoyer of those pleasures that lead to liberation. If one were to speak here figuratively, there is nothing at all that is more complete than this state of yours.
For even though his wealth was abundant, he desired to give it away again and again; he was patient, possessed constant strength, and was truly a son of power (Sahas);
he was worthy of renown, famous for his glory, and most highly celebrated.
He shall be a deliverer and bringer of booty (vāja) through his swift horses until the attainment of cattle;
moreover, O Brahmin, he shall be a donor through abundant giving.
He shall be a savior from battle, a giver of food, or a provider of enjoyment.

Whether engaged in battle with the senses through darkness or acting as a bestower of knowledge, you are the knower of praise; therefore, always maintain that awareness. For even though your knowledge is eternal, it is said that you "know" after having bestowed its fruit.
Or let this be a direct hymn of praise to You, the one who puts all afflictions to flight.
For he is truly great due to his immeasurability and possesses abundant happiness;
yet Garuḍa treats him with contempt, as if he were a mere comet, even though he belongs to Hari.
From this very sūtra, "tācchīlye maḥ," he is called "Dhūma" (the Smoky One).
May he grant us knowledge and food for those of virtuous deeds;
he who is the banner of the gods, the possessor of wealth, and the lord of the people.
May he of great splendor also hear our hymns.
Furthermore, the great gods headed by Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā, and the children headed by Skanda;
those very same ones who in some places appear in the form of young students, and these very same ones, Indra and the others, who appear as youths—[may they all hear us].
Their greatness arises from their qualities; compared to them, even Indra and the other gods are youths of middling merit.
And by comparison with those very qualities of theirs, even the Āśins and the Arbhakas are called "small.
Let us offer salutations to those who possess power; we do not merely withhold our praise for those who are superior. 138
Even for the single Viṣṇu, there exist distinctions of form, whether minute or great;
for even when youth is common to both, a distinction is made such as "the great youth" due to the difference in magnitude.
(139) Wherein the stones, extracted for the pressing, are vast and situated below—
O you for whom praise is accepted, come toward the Soma juices pressed by the *dhiṣaṇās*;
for from the root *guṝ*, meaning "to accept," the word *jalgula* denotes that which is worthy of praise.
Because the two pressing-boards resemble the hips of women, [the Soma is called] *phalaka-abhiṣuta*. 2.140.
When [the mantra] has been uttered, there is ascent and descent through the differentiation of conjunctions (saṅgati).
The tongue is the pressing-stone, and the application of speech is called the pressing (abhiṣava).
The mortar (khala) is the thigh, and the body is said to be Soma; the mind is the [priest].
And when knowledge arises, it is said to be at the lips, which are the place of the fruit (142).

Just as rays that are not fixed and rays that are fleeting are bound together in one place, so too the rays and the channels (nāḍīs) are joined elsewhere; for this reason, [the practitioner] is disciplined in every house.
Or rather, let him say "dehe dehe" (in body after body), or "dyumad dundubhimat" (resounding like a drum).
The Earth is his deity, or Hari himself residing therein;
another deity is said to be the Vanaspati, with Soma as his minister.
Soma, Viṣṇu, or Śruta is heard to be the deity of the fruit;
therefore, for all trees as well, [the deity resides] at the very top of the tree (vṛkṣāgra).
Or [the deity resides] in the wind that blows through the forests, or among the adorable celestial beings (divaukas).

Viṣṇu is her husband, and the god Vāyu indeed goes before him; for the sake of drinking his own Soma, or rather, O Viṣṇu, produce it by mind. They are the two who consume the supreme portion of the food obtained through sacrifice.
Just as from the root *bhakṣ* (to eat) we have "eater of horses" (*aśvabhakṣaka*) and "eater of food" (*annabhakṣaka*), so here [the two] are the drinkers of Soma; they are lofty, exceedingly great.
By the great pressers, let the honeyed Soma be pressed for Indra.
"Come here for the sake of purifying the Soma upon the filter over the wooden trough;
bring the remaining *ṛjīṣa* into the two cups, having placed it upon the cow's hide.
By saying "bring," he refers either to himself or to his inner controller (*antaryāmin*). (149)
The two skull-cups are said to be the Camasa vessels, and the belly is the Droṇa vessel;
the purifier here is indeed the intellect, for by it the mind is purified. The skin of the face itself is the Gocarma; thus, Viṣṇu resides within these.
Since we are like those who are blessed with excellent qualities, we must maintain this;
therefore, praise us in the matter of our pure speech, mind, and so forth.
O you of the great sacrifice, having made us possessed of much that is to be spoken and known— ||151||
O Lord of the waters, you who know all things, your deeds are everywhere renowned.
O Īśvara, although the Daityas, Rākṣasas, and Prajās are full of false views and are constantly ignorant, you cause them to sleep again and again in abundance.
May all those enemies of yours, perpetually deluded by ignorance, sleep forever;
and may your friends awaken to your truly fearless form.
O Lord, even as they praise you falsely with sinful illusion—
"Your qualities consist of illusion and do not exist in ultimate reality"—
thus constantly braying like a donkey known as a "proponent of illusion," crush him, casting him into the very darkness, for we are always tormented by him. 155–156.
And the wind cast them far down into that darkness;
that darkness, fierce with its biting cold, was called Kuṇḍṛṇācī because it was more wretched than even the depths of a pit (kuṇḍa). 157.
The syllable *kumbha* is designated as *kuṇḍa*; indeed, its destination is the Kumbhīpāka hell.
The letter *repha* and the transposition of vowels are stated for the purpose of indicating an intensification of that [punishment].
[Therefore,] slay and crush every sinner who utters slander behind one's back.
"Constantly bite him with dogs and other beasts, so that there may be a biting like that of *krakañcas*. O gods who are eager for booty and engaged in battle, or even you serpents,
sprinkle Indra with Soma, just as Krivi did for King Kṛti."
Or, like a creator or a Lord, Hari may have his own experience as an illustration;
or, like a drinker of a hundred or a thousand vessels of Soma mixed with milk, he never remains hidden anywhere. (2.160–161)
It dissolves those very things for the sake of this powerful intoxication;
they do not establish all the manifestations anywhere within its belly.
Due to its overflowing, it is called the "ocean," and due to its greatness, it is the primordial nature (prakṛti). 162.
This entire phenomenal world is yours alone, just as a pigeon [is contained] within its nest;
you pervade the universe perfectly, and therefore you bear our speech.
O bearer of words, your hymn encompasses all that is Vedic and Vedāntic.

"Let it be conceived thus: 'This speech of mine is truthful and pleasant, and this is my sovereign power. O Lord, let this be uttered through Your grace by granting the fruit [of my words], for You are the Supreme here in this battle consisting of both knowledge and ignorance. (164)
"Remain forever for the sake of accomplishing our desired purpose.
Abiding within me, you and I shall indeed speak to others:
'In every endeavor, we invoke that most resplendent Indra. (165–166)
"If he has been told, he will surely listen; and if he has heard, he will come.
Even with other intentions full of many purposes, he will respond to our call. Therefore, for the sake of that ancient dwelling place of Viṣṇu, I invoke Hari."
You are celebrated as the Great One, the Firm Foundation, and the Wide-Extending;
you whom the Creator Brahmā, your father, formerly invoked as "O Knower" or "O Devoted to You"—as such, we pray to you. 168–169.
O Soma-drinker, let that be so for us who are happy;
O God, act in such a way that we may obtain from them whatever we desire.
[2.170] Because *vajra* means knowledge and *vajra* means going, those who are endowed with wealth [are called Vajras].
The Revatīs are said to be cattle, abiding happily in the Sadhamāda.
The Tuvi-vājās possess great food and are endowed with stability;
there may be happiness joined with knowledge, or it may be our own powerful state under the Lord Satīśa.
May he be attained by you through you alone, as the one who desires praise from all sides;
moving and being moved by them, like the two wheels of a chariot in motion.
By virtue of being the support for the axle, may he fulfill the desire of those who offer praise.
Indra constantly conquered through the gods who, breathing fiercely out of anger and displaying their own prowess, stood all around him;
he was the giver of wealth to us, including the golden chariot, and having obtained it, he secured everything for our gain. || 174-175 ||
It should be like one possessing cattle and gold; for us, it is exactly as it has come to be.
It is like a horse joined with happiness and sons, for from which there is well-being and ease. From the name "Aśva" (Horse), [it yields] *iḍ* (prosperity), sovereignty, a hero, and heroic power.
The cow is speech, which is beneficial and supremely delightful; it is the Supreme Brahman, exalted by its qualities.
This chariot, which is your own body, is joined with the yoga of the Sama-veda;
because it consists of consciousness and bliss, it is known as immortal in the ocean of milk.
To the extent that liberation is attained, it is called equal yoga (samāna-yoga).
There is one wheel on the summit of the mountain, fixed and moving in the sky;
there is the wheel of evil for the slayer of Hari, and the wheel of merit above the divine one.
What mortal could serve for your enjoyment, since you are dear to all?
For what reason would you be dear to anyone, when you are full of bliss and have no desire for anything? And for the sake of what self-interest do you go anywhere?
Due to his specific manifestation, Viṣṇu is called Vibhāvarī (the Night).
We meditate upon you alone, whose limit and supreme power are the entire universe;
the supreme power is indeed great bliss, while Śrī is within, and Kali is proclaimed to be at the end. 181–182.
O Goddess, when the dawn has arisen for both hell and heaven, it is always auspicious like a noble horse, O fair one, as it breathes forth its light;
because it is manifested by that [dawn], it is likewise called Hari, the son of Heaven. 183

With devotion, he praised Acyuta, who resides in the directions of Agni, Indra, and the others, even though He exists separately; while praising Viṣṇu— the eternal one known as Svarṇa, whose beautiful body is like gold— he attained the fame of being called Svarṇastūpa.
Having seen him, he became honored by others and attained true knowledge.
In Aṅga, Raso became a seer through that very knowledge; Hari became the beloved friend of the gods;
and by your vow alone, the Maruts became possessed of great wisdom, endowed with learning and action.
Pervading the universe and endowed with supreme wisdom, the one who reclines upon the ocean likewise perceives both the inert and the conscious;
for though he appears in many forms, he is indeed the Lord, the Teacher, the eternal Friend, and the Father of all creatures.
O Viṣṇu, you first manifested from Mātariśvan because of his great clarity of understanding.
Vāyu and Vivasvat shone because they dwelt in various places; Śrī and Bhū graced the one who offers all oblations.
By virtue of your boon, the two worlds (rodasī) were split from your tooth; for that single [world] indeed became divided into two.
No one at all can withstand him, for neither Vāyu nor Viriñca, nor even Mahat, could destroy him.
You have entrusted the burden of the universe to him, and because you dwell everywhere, you are the Vasu.
To Manu and Vāyu, who possess distinguished awakening, you gave the beloved heaven in the form of knowledge, O God, so that the entire world might indeed have its voice as his own. 188–189.
Purūravas is indeed Vāyu, because of the word *uru* (wide/great), or because he performs good deeds for others who are well-doers.
Vāyu is indeed *śvā*, from *śvasana* (breathing) and *trāṇataḥ* (protecting); he is eternally liberated from both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
By him alone did the ancient sages bring you here, and again have others brought you with great devotion. (2.190)
"You are to be constantly heard by the sacrificer, O Eternal One, when you have entered among the people at the head of life;
the Veda declares that the six qualities beginning with sovereignty, which abide eternally, constitute the meaning of the *vaṣaṭ* call.
When the assembly known as true knowledge has arisen, you deliver even a man of sinful conduct."
Once, while wandering in his own home among various offspring, the far-seeing Lord, the master of heroes, was present in the battle for booty;
when the time for acquisition had come and the goal was to be attained, even those who were few took refuge in you.
For when they approached there in accordance with Truth, even though they were many, you destroyed them by your power or by your numbers without effort. (192–193)
Day after day, desiring to hear that praise, you establish the one who praises you in immortality;

out of excessive affection, being thirsty for that [praise], you extend happiness to both humans and gods alike, especially to the wise man there, for whom you are eternally dear and for whom you are thirsting for the bliss known as liberation. 194.
For the sake of our acquisition of the wealth of wisdom, may you make us illustrious, skillful, and givers of knowledge.
By performing acts such as worship until they become direct perception, one is called a *kāru*—a seer of reality.
Being praised for his new work, may we attain prosperity through that which was done previously. 195
You are ever present beside our parents, Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as their controller; among the gods, you are the vigilant, eternal knower. O best of the wise, awaken us, who have fashioned these bodies!
You bestow all wealth upon the singer, and we, along with you, are your brothers, the makers of life. 196.
Because he dwells within this single body like a child in a womb, the Jīva is eternally his brother.
Because he impels the vital breath (āyuḥ) within the heart of King Nahuṣa, he is called Āyus;
and the gods, through the very act of creating his body, gave that name to the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) who resides within the Jīva.
Vāsudeva indeed possesses both name and object; for that reason, he is called Āyu first here by virtue of his power (śakti).

Manu is his name, and Ilā was his daughter; this [name] belongs to Viṣṇu eternally because of his being worthy of praise (ilaṇīyatva) and his being the source of subsistence (upajīvyatva), and because he is the vehicle of life (āyurayana) and knowledge. || 198–199 ||
Because she is to be instructed, Mānavī is the one to be taught; because he is the instructor, Vāsudeva is the teacher.
For a son belongs to a father who exercises ownership, and independence is nothing other than ownership.
O God, protect us—the bodies of us, your worshippers—by means of your own powers of protection.

By the word "and" (ca), [knowledge, devotion, and so forth] are also [included]; truly, you are always the victor over us. 201. You are the protector of our offspring and our son, because you are the continuity of this child;
and you are the guardian of our cows, of knowledge, happiness, and speech, and indeed, without blinking, [you protect] the gods as well. 202.
Protecting [the sacrifice] through them when it has proceeded, you are indeed the protector and the inner witness of the two sacrifices;
for you, who are utterly free from attachment and without a bow (or weapon), you shine with the vision of knowledge through devotion.
Because of having two heads, he is four-eyed as the Adhiyajña; "two heads" refers to speech, as will be stated later.
To him who offers oblations for the sake of great peace and for the satisfaction of the performer, you indeed grant the desired mantra;
to him who utters a great hymn of praise, you bestow the cherished, desirable wealth and supreme happiness.
You are proclaimed as the giver of wisdom and as the Father, even unto Vāyu, the sustainer who flows everywhere.

You govern the entire realm whose administrative duties have reached full maturity; because you are a local ruler, you are a most excellent knower [of affairs]. (205) Like a suit of armor, you constantly wear [the burden of duty] through diligent effort, you who give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in the sacrifices.
In the home, you provide for others a pleasant dwelling, delicious food, and a comfortable residence, creating for them a state of ease that is truly restful. (206)

For one who, having made a firm vow, performs sacrifice throughout their entire life, that very [vow] leads to the attainment of heaven; for in this state, the body itself is the vessel, or rather, it is the dwelling on the path of knowledge. 207. Let there be no anger toward me, thinking that this taking of refuge in you is a small matter of endurance.
I have traveled far for the sake of attaining you, and having attained you, my father—the giver of knowledge to the gods—is reached.
O Lord, you are the one who causes humans to wander and likewise the creator of sages through the granting of knowledge.
Just as Manu, Aṅgiras, or Yayāti came to your abode, so too has my house come to you.
Come hither, bring the assembly of gods, and seat them upon the sacred grass; perform the sacrifice that is dear to You.
Since You alone are the sacrificer dwelling within all living beings, manifest Yourself through the words of the Veda.
Whatever we have done for You with our power, whether knowingly or otherwise—grant us prosperity and well-being, and lead us toward Your gracious wisdom.
O Lord, always unite us with that enjoyment, for by that power we have performed your good deed.
(Sūkta 1.32,
Head Recitation, Head Recitation)

I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra—or indeed of Vāsudeva—those which he performed as his principal acts. Now I shall declare the heroic deeds of Indra, those which the wielder of the thunderbolt performed for the first time:
he slew the serpent Daitya and the Doubter; with his foot, he cleared the path. He struck down Ahi and pierced the waters; he split open the bellies of the mountains.

He shattered the obstacles, or [shattered] the days according to his actions; he struck down the days and he shattered the waters. Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned this thunderbolt of knowledge for him, which Viriñca fashioned as having that as its object—that which consists of light.
Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for him a celestial thunderbolt; a celestial thunderbolt, sharpened, or born of sound—Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for him a celestial thunderbolt.

Like cows with young calves, like lowing milch-cows, these waters, thus impelled, have flowed straight toward the ocean; they have gone straight to the ocean. Just as a thirsty bull seeks the Soma, he drank it at the three libations. Acting like a bull, he chose the Soma and drank of the pressed juice at the Trikadruka rites.
The Soma juices became swift at the pressings when the mind was directed toward meditation; acting like a bull, Indra chose the Soma and drank of the pressed juice at the Trikadruka rites.

You slew him, the foremost of the deceivers, and you destroyed their deceptive forms and illusions. When, O Indra, you struck down the first-born of the great ones and annihilated the wiles of the deceivers, from that moment you became the maker of the sun and the days; by your very power, you had no enemy. Having generated the sun, the sky, and the dawn, you truly found no adversary at all.

I have struck down Vṛtra, who was shoulderless and even more than that—darkness and false conviction—because of his mutilation. Indra struck down Vṛtra, the worse-than-Vṛtra, with his great thunderbolt, his deadly weapon.

Just as shoulders are severed, so too was the serpent mangled by the thunderbolt for the sake of the clan. Like shoulders severed by a bolt, the serpent lies prostrate, pressed close against the earth.
Knowledge is indeed the thunderbolt of Name, while Intellect is called Earth; that which resides therein is doubt.
He whose warrior is no non-warrior is like Indra’s enemy; for like one who does not fight, the intoxicated one challenged him.
I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of either Indra or Vāsudeva, those which he performed as his chief acts:
he slew the serpent-demon Ahi and, with the Janālu-sāra weapon, he carved out a path. 211.
He shattered obstacles by means of his actions, or rather, he carried away the difficult-to-speak words of those with wings (or: of the sides) through their movement;
and as for the life-breaths of living beings possessing the stages of birth, he indeed pierced them with excellent arguments.
Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned this thunderbolt of knowledge, while Viriñca fashioned that which has this as its object and whose nature is splendor.
Like cows with their calves lowing toward a sharp, thunderous vajra born of sound,
or like waters flowing straight to the ocean, so do these utterances go toward this exalted God;
just as a thirsty bull chooses and drinks the Soma at the three libations.
The Soma juices, which are swift and of a dark-red hue during the libations, have here directed the mind toward the yoga of meditation;
thus he has taken up that very knowledge which effects dissolution and brings about the evening [of worldly existence], or rather, he has resolved his doubt like the Lord.
He slew this first of the deceivers and destroyed their deceptive forms and illusions.

Therefore, you alone are the creator of the sun, the days, and so forth; by your power, you do not encounter an enemy, or else you have destroyed the illusion of those who speak with deceit through the victory of your own people. You slew Vṛtra and Vyaṃsa, and even more than that, you destroyed darkness and false conviction because of that act of destruction.
Just as a mountain peak when shattered, or as a serpent struck by a thunderbolt at the command of the clan;

just as knowledge is the thunderbolt for one named Kuliśa, and wisdom is indeed called the earth—so too is doubt that resides therein. Therefore, he whose warrior is joined with the earth is not a non-warrior; such is Indra’s enemy.

Indeed, intoxicated by pride, Vṛtra challenged Śakra or Viṣṇu—the foremost of heroes among enemies—out of ignorance. For the sake of stability, he sought the destroyer of the great ones known as Ṛjīṣa; yet he did not attain the knowledge of Viṣṇu’s slaying. Furthermore, Vṛtra overstepped Śakra’s bounds and crushed the subjects.
"Indra-śatru" refers to one for whom Indra is the enemy; that is, he who possesses an enemy that is Indra.
According to the ancient rule, "In a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in a masculine word with a preceding [member], the final vowel is circumflex (svarita)," [the form is established].
Even though his feet and arms were completely severed, he fought against Indra alone; he hurled the thunderbolt at him.

Upon his neck, which resembled the ridge of a mountain, Viṣṇu struck with the thunderbolt of his hand the darkness that was devoid of both logic and scripture—a darkness fit for slaughter, lowly, and worthy of death.
Desiring to become an enemy of the Lord, he was shattered and lay prostrate in many pieces by that Lord. (2.220–221)
By that same means, along with his own measure and with Śakra, he struck down the obstructer of the waters as he lay there;
and just as the waters flow forth after a river has been breached, so too do they proceed, having first taken possession of the mind.

Vṛtra, who formerly stood encompassing those waters by his own greatness, and the serpent who was his son—[of those two... 222. [Note: The provided Sanskrit fragment for verse 222 appears to be incomplete or corrupted; the translation above reflects the standard interpretation of the preceding context.]
Immediately after Pāda, Śīr was born; likewise, Abhirundan was born from him.
Saṃśaya, the son of Tamas, or rather Abhirundan, remained there performing auspicious deeds, but he too was slain by him.
Danu, the mother of Vṛtra and the Dānavas, who brings about bondage even in a lowly place, is she indeed.
For Vṛtra was indeed a Danuja born from Kaśyapa, while that evil-souled one was a Vaiṣṇava born of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Since Vṛtra was her son, she was called "Vṛtraputrā" (the mother of Vṛtra); Indra first took away her life.
Or rather, Vṛtra’s mother was Prakṛti, for darkness (tamas) belonged to her; the Lord (Īśitā) slew her.
It is fitting that the individual nature, as well as darkness and other defects, belong to the person.
For the sake of her son, Aditi remained above him; having struck down that [Vṛtra], Indra slew him [Viṣṇu]. By destroying the cause itself, Viṣṇu prevented the arising of the effect.
Thus indeed there would first be the destruction of the effect, and then the total destruction of the cause itself through its own dissolution.
In this way, Lord Nārāyaṇa graced his devotees, delivering them from the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsṛti).
Furthermore, the state of being "higher" than primordial nature (prakṛti) arises from His power; because He is infinite, no limits can ever be established for Him.
Therefore, they have no secret dwelling place; the waters move with ease.
Vṛtra reached that long darkness known as Vṛtra, or rather, he himself became that long, blinding darkness. The wives of Varuṇa, the subduer of Dāsa, were confined just as if by a serpent.
In the battle with Bala at Indra’s sacrifice, Śakra swiftly slew Vṛtra and that serpent;
then the Blessed One, like the sun destroying darkness, opened the auspicious gateway to the waters.
If even the preeminent god had been your opponent in that hand-to-hand combat, he would have become your horseman.
Indeed, you were like Vālin at that time; for there was no one who could strike you back.
Thus, by your might, you conquered the cows, you conquered the gold, you released Soma, and you set free the seven rivers.
You [overcame] the thunderbolt, the lightning, the mist, and the weapon named Miha, which is as sharp as a sacrificial blade.
That fierce serpent hurled at you alone that thunderbolt known by the name Hrāduni;
yet it found no success against you, for in later times you yourself were born from him.
O Indra, whom did you see as a warrior of the serpent, that even he felt fear when you slew him?

When the Supreme Lord is favorable to His interlocutor, [the following occur]: from false awakening arise various cognitions; my mind abandons sound and the other objects of sense, like the seven oceans;
the intellect and the other principles (mahat-tattva etc. are perceived erroneously; the lightning-like sound is the power of the speaker;

This one, the commander of an entire army, destroys enemies and darkness without remainder;

Bestowing abundant reality upon his devotee and granting great welfare, may you never at any time become a demon.

you have slain the one who is a mass of ignorance through knowledge, and the one who sacrifices only for wealth.

As for the other sacrificers who will be mentioned later, they are the Asuras who vied with the sacrificers.
Even they abandoned their own heads, their purpose fulfilled merely by emulating the virtuous;
you, however, being steadfast and a master of your senses, cast them down from heaven to the earth for violating their vows.

perished like warriors skilled in slaying their own enemies, though they were themselves destroyed by those who leaped upon them.

Indeed, by their own qualities or by the qualities of Viṣṇu, through the grace of the Lord, they went along destroying [the obstacles]. You alone fought against the hosts of Rākṣasas who were devouring the sages and those who were being oppressed and weeping;

The God of gods fashioned knowledge as his weapon, indeed as a thunderbolt, to slay the Dasyus; by his own light, he certainly destroys the darkness residing in the hearts of his devotees. That which is ignorance is itself knowledge for Viṣṇu, whose actions, though fierce, result only in bliss.

Paṅktirādha is Hari; he alone is the hero and the benefactor of men.
The gods, Gandharvas, ancestors, and Daityas are designated as the five classes of beings (pañcajanāḥ).
To the one who praises him, Viṣṇu grants excellent wealth.
That by which a man becomes truly excellent is called *sunara*, knowledge. He who offers this sustenance (*anna*) attains imperishable fame.
Because of its great vigor, it is *suvīra*; it is swift in action and well-fashioned in form.
Because he is the cause of the movement of the vital breaths, he is said to be "here" (iha);

By virtue of being the one who causes [the self] to arise, that very Lord Hari is the Uktha. 3.141–142.
We shall recite that very mantra, which expresses those deities and those divine powers denoted by it—the cause of happiness for the sake of knowledge.

Who could obtain a devotee of the gods, so exceedingly difficult to find?
Or who could follow a sacrificer who has properly spread the sacrificial grass?
As that sacrificer proceeds from place to place, he himself is filled with happiness.
Since Viṣṇu is present within one's own desired locations,
by worshipping Him with knowledge through that very presence, one attains a state of imperishability.
That Janārdana is joined with the Kṣatriyas through His pervasive entry.
With them, the god slays his enemies and provides refuge for himself in times of fear.
There is no one who can withstand him, overcome him, surpass him, or conquer him.
For battle is indeed a great prize, and wealth is well known as the very object of desire.
